publications.title: Exploring the Relationship Between Adolescent Fertility Rates and Pediatric Antiretroviral Treatment Coverage in Countries Across Sub-Saharan Africa
publications.description: Co-authored a public-health research paper examining the relationship between adolescent fertility rates and pediatric antiretroviral treatment coverage across 34 Sub-Saharan African countries. Our team analyzed international health data using linear regression, the Shapiro-Wilk test, a one-tailed two-sample t-test, Cohen’s d, and confounder analysis. posts.text: A button that wouldn’t stop glowing taught me something useful about AI video. I’ve just completed Higgsfield Academy’s “AI Creation: First Steps.” Certificate attached. 🧩 In one practice scene, an engineer presses a prototype’s button. The light is supposed to pulse once. Instead, it stays on. The character looks convincing. The camera move works. But that tiny continuity error changes what the viewer understands. But “conversation to completed task” would be the wrong description of what the recording shows. I’d rather see the actual handoff: here’s what the software produced, here’s what the person did, and here’s the result. The same goes for a demo with prepared inputs. A voice agent can finish a call without finishing the job. That’s the problem Jose Cruz-Lopez and I are working through with June at Anticipation Labs during Stan Launchpad. Suppose the task is to move an appointment. The agent dials the right number, navigates the phone tree, and leaves a clear voicemail. The call succeeded. The appointment hasn’t moved. We’re building an AI assistant you can reach from a landline. No app to download. No dashboard to learn. Her name is June. Jose C. and I are building her at Anticipation Labs during Stan Launchpad, for older adults who would rather talk on the phone than navigate another screen. Start with an ordinary request: “Could you call the clinic and ask about moving my appointment?” The person has explained what they need. Jose wrote about the grandparents who raised him. That’s the part of this story I want people to remember. June starts with a belief I care about: you shouldn’t have to learn another app just to get help with everyday life. For older adults who would rather pick up the phone, we want that phone call to be enough. I’m in my first semester at Western. You can drive a yacht on my portfolio. Yes, this is still a website about my work. Meet Open Water. 🚤 I love the water, boats and yachts, and I wanted my personal website to actually feel personal. So I turned it into an ocean you can explore. Take the helm. Explore the islands. Head beneath the surface into reefs and caves. There’s even a dolphin called Dakota. Some of my week is spent building Anticipy. Some of it is spent calculating a parking bill in Python. I’m in first-year computer science at Western, and one of my assignments is a parking duration and cost calculator. It takes a licence plate, arrival and departure times, and a parking rate. Then it needs to turn that into a clear result. There isn’t a particularly glamorous way to describe it. But there’s plenty to understand: which values are text, which are numbers, how the calculation works,

At Launchpad, I want to test Anticipy before I explain it. A pitch gives me a lot of control. I choose the example, explain the context, and steer around the parts that need work. A product test should give some of that control away. My goal is to put a prototype in front of someone with a task they actually need to complete, then watch before walking them through the solution. Where do they hesitate?
